To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is no strong evidence of the effectiveness of mathematics curriculum materials, computer-assisted instruction, or mathematics textbooks in improving achievement in middle school and high school.

(a) there is a small but consistent effect for cooperative learning, (b) there is a very small effect for computer assisted instruction, (c) there is no effect for mathematics curricula, (d) there is no evidence that the effects of these programs vary for students with differing backgrounds, and (e) the evidence for these programs is based on a small number of studies.
there are few mathematics programs that work, and that the ones that do are not widely used in the United States.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of mathematical understanding and the ability to use that understanding to solve mathematical problems.
how the mathematics curriculum is taught, and not with what is taught.
the development of mathematical thinking and the learning of mathematics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the research base for middle and high school mathematics programs is not as strong as it is for elementary school programs and is not yet strong enough to support the development of specific recommendations for mathematics programs in these grades.

, in general, there is little evidence that any particular mathematics program is superior to any other, and there is little evidence of the effectiveness of any program in the middle and high school mathematics literature.
, in general, there are no programs in middle or high school mathematics that have been shown to have a positive effect on achievement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence base is strongest for the use of small group cooperative learning in mathematics classrooms and for using the same instructional approach for all groups of students.
the evidence base on effective mathematics programs in middle and high schools is much smaller and weaker than the evidence base on elementary school mathematics programs.
the evidence is not very promising for mathematics programs in the middle school and high school years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have a lot more work to do.
there is a dearth of research on mathematics education in the middle school years, and the studies we found had a variety of methodological shortcomings.
there are no magic bullet programs.
